quiz.q: What does a trait definition actually contain?
options: Field declarations only
Method signatures (and optionally default bodies) describing behavior a type promises to provide
A list of concrete types allowed to use it
Compiled machine code shared between types
quiz.explain: A trait lists method signatures — the shape of the promise. A type keeps that promise by writing an `impl Trait for Type` block.

quiz.q: You wrote `trait Greet { fn hello(&self) -> String; }` but never wrote `impl Greet for Dog`. What happens when you call `dog.hello()`?
options: It compiles and returns an empty string
It compiles using a default implementation
Compile error: no method named 'hello' found for 'Dog'
It panics at runtime
quiz.explain: A trait alone does nothing for a type. Without an impl block, Dog never kept the promise, so the compiler can't find the method.

quiz.q: In a trait definition, what's the difference between `fn hello(&self) -> String;` and `fn hello(&self) -> String { ... }`?
options: No difference, both are required methods
The first is a required method (implementers must write it); the second is a default method (implementers get it for free unless they override it)
The first is faster at runtime
The second can only be used with generics
quiz.explain: A `;` means no body — every implementer must supply one. A body in the trait itself is a default that implementers inherit automatically.

quiz.q: What is the effect of a default method in a trait?
options: It forces every implementer to override it
It provides behavior automatically to any type that implements the trait, unless that type chooses to override it
It only works for the first type that implements the trait
It removes the need for an impl block entirely
quiz.explain: Types that implement the trait get the default method's behavior for free — they only need to write it themselves if they want different behavior.

quiz.q: `fn f<T>(x: T) { x.summarize(); }` fails to compile with 'no method named summarize found for type parameter T'. Why?
options: summarize() doesn't exist anywhere in the program
T has no trait bound, so the compiler has no information that T has a summarize method
Generic functions can never call methods
x needs to be borrowed with &
quiz.explain: An unbounded generic type parameter could be literally anything. Without `T: Summary`, the compiler can't assume summarize() exists.

quiz.q: When must you use `fn f<T: Trait>(x: T, y: T)` instead of `fn f(x: &impl Trait, y: &impl Trait)`?
options: Never, they are always interchangeable
When you need to guarantee x and y are the same concrete type
When the trait has default methods
When the function returns a value
quiz.explain: `impl Trait` sugar creates an independent anonymous type per parameter, so it can't express 'same T twice.' The generic form with a named T can.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a `where` clause on a generic function?
options: It changes the runtime behavior of the function
It's purely a readability tool — it expresses the exact same bounds as `<T: ...>`, just moved below the signature
It allows bounds that `<T: Trait>` cannot express
It's required whenever a function has more than one type parameter
quiz.explain: `where` clauses are syntactic sugar for the same bounds you could put inline in `<...>`. They exist to keep signatures with multiple/combined bounds readable.

quiz.q: Why is it misleading to think of a trait as a 'base class'?
options: Traits can only be implemented once per program
Traits describe capabilities ('can do'), not an inheritance hierarchy ('is a'), and carry no data of their own
Traits cannot have default methods
Traits are only used for printing
quiz.explain: A type can implement many unrelated traits with none of them being a 'parent.' Traits are behavior contracts, not a place to store fields.

quiz.q: A trait method has `&self` as its first parameter. What does that mean?
options: The method takes ownership of the value it's called on
The method borrows the value it's called on, without taking ownership
The method is static and needs no instance
The method can only be called once
quiz.explain: `&self` borrows the receiver, the same way any other `&` reference borrows a value — the caller keeps ownership.

flashcards.back: A named list of method signatures a type promises to provide — a behavior contract, not inheritance.

flashcards.front: How does a type keep a trait's promise?
flashcards.back: By writing `impl TraitName for TypeName { ... }` with real bodies for each required method.

flashcards.front: Required method vs default method in a trait definition — how do you tell them apart?
flashcards.back: Required: signature ends in `;`, no body — implementers must write it. Default: signature has a `{ ... }` body — implementers get it free, can override it.

flashcards.front: Two equivalent ways to write a trait-bounded function parameter.
flashcards.back: `fn f(x: &impl Trait)` (sugar) and `fn f<T: Trait>(x: &T)` (explicit generic) — same meaning for a single parameter.

flashcards.front: When do you need `<T: Trait>` instead of `impl Trait` sugar?
flashcards.back: When the same type parameter must appear more than once and be guaranteed identical each time, e.g. `fn cmp<T: PartialEq>(a: T, b: T)`.

flashcards.front: What does a `where` clause do that inline `<T: Bound>` doesn't?
flashcards.back: Nothing functionally — it's the same bounds, just written below the signature for readability once there are multiple bounds or type parameters.

flashcards.front: What error do you get calling a trait method on an unbounded generic `T`?
flashcards.back: "no method named '...' found for type parameter 'T'" — the fix is adding the trait bound, e.g. `<T: Summary>`.

flashcards.front: "Can do" vs "is a" — which describes traits?
flashcards.back: "Can do." Traits are capabilities a type has, not a parent-child inheritance relationship, and they carry no fields.
